messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin is a 55-year-old single man of European descent who works as a counselor at a community mental health center. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, seeking help for the first time following a man-made disaster that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Martin was present at a warehouse fire caused by an industrial accident in his neighborhood — a fire that spread rapidly and with terrifying speed, trapping several people inside. He was among the bystanders who attempted to help, pulling a woman through a broken window while the structure groaned and smoke poured in thick, acrid waves around them. The smell of burning material — synthetic, chemical, nothing like a campfire — saturated his clothes and hair for days afterward. At one point, a panicked man nearby hurled a fire extinguisher across the pavement in desperation, the clatter of metal on concrete cutting through the roar of the flames. Martin made it out. Not everyone did.

In the weeks that followed, Martin noticed that the smell of smoke — from a neighbor's fireplace, from a passing vehicle's exhaust, from anything that carried even a faint char — would stop him cold. The burnt smell in particular, so specific to that afternoon, seemed to reach inside him and pull something loose. These olfactory triggers did not merely remind him of the event; they transported him into the emotional core of it, flooding him with fear and helplessness before he had time to register what was happening. Similarly, the sound or sight of objects being thrown — even a colleague setting down a heavy binder with a thud — could produce the same sudden activation. As these triggers began to surface memory, Martin found himself caught in fragmentary, disorienting recall: not clear images, but the smell of that smoke arising unbidden during the memory itself, and waves of raw emotional intensity that arrived without any accompanying picture, as though the terror had been encoded separately from everything else. Perhaps most unsettling to him was the quality of the memory itself — it felt, he told his intake clinician, like something that had happened to a stranger, like footage from someone else's life that he had somehow absorbed. He could not make it feel like his own.

Martin had come to believe, with quiet but firm conviction, that his body had turned against him — that its continued alarm responses were evidence of something broken and unreliable. He was certain that he had to stay vigilant at all times, because the disaster had proven to him that catastrophe could arrive without warning. These appraisals did not sit passively alongside his memory; they actively colored it, lending every recollection a quality of ongoing threat, as though the danger had never truly ended. And in turn, the memory reinforced these beliefs — each intrusive wave of emotion without image seemed to confirm that he was not processing things normally, that something was fundamentally wrong with him.

To manage this, Martin had developed a set of strategies that made intuitive sense to him but were quietly narrowing his life. He had stopped seeing friends, partly because social gatherings sometimes involved fireplaces or candles, and partly because he feared losing control of his reactions in front of others. He had made a determined effort to avoid thinking about the event at all, believing — with some force — that if he allowed himself to dwell on it, he would not be able to cope, that he would unravel entirely. But suppressing thought about the event had an ironic consequence: the memories became more intrusive, more fragmentary, and more emotionally raw, as though the material that had never been processed kept pressing back against the door he had shut. He had also begun monitoring his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance, scanning for any sign that he was losing his grip on sanity. This constant internal surveillance left him little cognitive room for anything else.

At work, the strain had become impossible to ignore. Martin counsels clients who have experienced trauma, and the work now costs him enormously — a client describing a fire in a session, or the faint smell of smoke drifting in from outside the building's ventilation system, could destabilize him for the rest of the afternoon. He had begun scheduling fewer clients and leaving early on difficult days, and his supervisor had noticed. It was this — the fear that his professional life, the one domain that had always anchored him, was slipping — that finally brought Martin to seek help. What he is most afraid of is that the damage is permanent. What he most hopes is that he can feel, once again, like the events of that day belong to him — and that he might be able to bear them.
